newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Merger creates new shipping giant.
newsitem.headline: Merger creates new shipping giant.

text.p: Britain's The Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co. and the Netherlands' Nedlloyd Groep on Monday announced a merger in container shipping that will put them in the world's top four container fleets and lead to cost savings of $200 million a year.

Nedlloyd and P&O will each take a 50 percent stake in a new company joining their container shipping interests, to be called P&O Nedlloyd Container Line. Nedlloyd will pay P&O $175 million to equalise the shareholdings.

The merger will create the world's largest container company in terms of fleet size, or standing container slots, and the third in terms of business volume, behind Maersk and Evergreen and alongside Sea-Land at 2.3 million 20-foot equivalent units, or TEUs, per year. The TEU is the standard measure of volume in container shipping.
The companies said savings of more than $200 million a year had already been identified from a total $3.9 billion cost base.
The savings will be achieved by eliminating up to 1,400 jobs from an existing combined work force of about 9,400, greater network efficiency and reduced inland and terminal costs.

P&O Nedlloyd, to be jointly chaired by Lord Sterling of P&O and Leo Berndsen of Nedlloyd, will begin operations by the end of the year following "due diligence" investigations and regulatory procedures.

Headquartered in London but with its fleet managed from Rotterdam in the Netherlands, the new company will operate 112 owned and chartered container ships and 540,000 TEU of owned and leased container boxes.

Analysts praised the merger plans. In an industry with strong potential economies of scale, analysts said it was inevitable that companies move beyond large alliances to outright mergers and, as the first in the sector to do so, Nedlloyd and P&O would be the first to reap cost savings, and benefit from complementary routes worldwide.

"The cost savings are very much higher than Nedlloyd has so far been making with its Global Alliance. I'm very positive, but of course the competition will not disappear because of this," said Pieter van Gelder, analyst at Delta Lloyd Bank.
ING Baring Research immediately upgraded Nedlloyd's stock from a sell to a buy.

"We view this move as the best long-term move for Nedlloyd in order to survive in the price-cutting environment of the container shipping market," said ING Baring's head of equity research, Thibaud de Guerre.
However, analysts were left wondering about the future of P&O's and Nedlloyd's respective worldwide shipping alliances.

Nedlloyd works within a global shipping consortium with American President Lines, Mitsui OSK Lines and Orient Overseas Container Line. P&O's alliance groups Hapag-Lloyd, Neptune Orient Lines of Singapore and Nippon Yusen Kaisha.
"They can't be in both alliances. There will have to be some reshuffling," said Gert Jochems, analyst at NIB Strating Securities.
Nedlloyd will take a 200 million guilder ($120 million) extraordinary charge this year to cover the effects of the merger.

Finance director Haddo Meijer said the charge would result from a writedown in the value of ships that will be transferred to the newly formed venture, partially offsetting first-half extraordinary gains of 273 million guilders ($164 million), largely the result of the sale of Nedlloyd's offshore drilling unit, Neddrill.
